_: Research about a KIND of product, not a brand. Section 1 calls this `class` scope and section 4 says it transfers to every SKU sharing the mechanism, including across brands. It could only ever warn: rule 1.1 means a class study can never clear a product, only a test of the actual product does that. Each finding must name what escapes it, because a finding every product in a category carries tells a shopper nothing (rule 5.3, and the Sonicare mistake).

findings.headline: Tea bags with a plastic seam or mesh release 11.6 billion microplastic particles per cup
findings.detail: A single hot brew of a plastic mesh tea bag releases an estimated 11.6 billion microplastic and 3.1 billion nanoplastic particles into one cup. Paper bags are commonly sealed with polypropylene; pyramid mesh styles are often nylon or PET.
findings.source: McGill University, Environmental Science and Technology, 2019
findings.escapeNote: Loose leaf and paper only bags have no seam to shed.

findings.headline: Polypropylene baby bottles release up to 16.2 million microplastic particles per litre at formula temperature
findings.detail: Polypropylene bottles, about 82 percent of the global market, release 1.3 to 16.2 million particles per litre in hot water at formula preparation temperature. Shaking increases release; sterilising with boiling water is highest of all.
findings.escapeNote: Glass, stainless and silicone bottles are not the polymer that was measured.

findings.headline: Bottled water carries roughly 240,000 plastic particles per litre
findings.detail: Laser microscopy counted about 240,000 plastic particles per litre across popular bottled water brands, roughly 90 percent of them nanoplastics, far above typical treated tap water. PET sheds faster with heat and time, so storage matters.
findings.escapeNote: Nothing sold as bottled water escapes this, which is the point: the alternative is not another bottle.
findings.alternative: Tap water through a filter, or water sold in glass.

findings.headline: Roughly a third of period underwear tested carried intentionally added PFAS
findings.detail: Independent testing found organic fluorine as high as 940 ppm in some Thinx styles and 373 ppm in a Knix style. Others in the same category tested non detect, so this is not a property of the category, and an untested pair cannot be placed on either side of it.
findings.escapeNote: A published non detect for organic fluorine answers this directly.

findings.headline: Sea salt is the most microplastic contaminated salt, because it is evaporated seawater
findings.detail: A study of 39 salt brands from 21 countries detected microplastics in roughly 90 percent of them, and sea salt was the most contaminated category. Independent testing puts sea salt at around 681 particles per kilogram against about 204 for salt mined from underground deposits. The mechanism is the source rather than the brand: seawater carries the ocean's plastic, and evaporating it concentrates what was already there. This is about sea salt generally. We have not confirmed it for any individual product.
findings.source: Environmental Science & Technology, 39 brands across 21 countries
findings.escapeNote: Salt mined from an underground deposit is not evaporated seawater and does not carry this. That is the alternative outside the category, and it is what we recommend.

_guard: A finding must name what escapes it. Usually that is a sibling in the same category: loose leaf has no bag, glass is not the measured polymer. Where the whole category carries it, the finding must instead name an alternative outside the category, or it is a fact about the world rather than a way to tell two products apart, and it belongs in an article.
